Deliberately Unfinished: On Growth as a Practice

By Furaihan Kamyl Arnazaye · 2026 · 3 min read

I have a folder of certificates. Seminars attended, online courses completed, credentials added to a LinkedIn profile. None of them is what I mean when I talk about growth.

What I mean is building systems that close real gaps, sustaining them over time, and accepting that the work is never fully done.

Two years into this career, first as an intern navigating multi-stakeholder policy environments and then as a full-time analyst, I have worked across levels I did not expect this early. Think-tank researchers, university lecturers and deans, legislative advisors, C-level executives. Policy negotiations that required analytical depth and interpersonal precision at the same time. Moments where reading the room mattered as much as the quality of the brief. I have handled most of those situations well. But "well" is not the standard I am working toward.

What I keep coming back to is a specific kind of professional. Someone who can enter any room, at any level, and communicate with clarity, credibility, and the right kind of presence. I know what the distance between where I am and where I want to be looks like.

The most important shift in how I think about closing that distance was treating it the way I treat research. With a question, a method, and a feedback loop. The question is never "how do I get better." That is too vague to act on. The questions I find useful are specific. What does executive presence actually consist of, and which components am I already demonstrating? Where does my verbal delivery break down relative to my written output?

The method is deliberate input. Books, research, and direct observation of professionals I respect, combined with reflection after real interactions. The feedback loop closes when I pay attention to what landed and what did not, then adjust. Three things are open right now:

  • The mechanics of executive presence. How to signal credibility before you speak, how to hold a position under pressure without becoming rigid, and how to make a short contribution carry more weight than a long one.
  • Interpersonal communication across contexts. The register, framing, and pace of a conversation need to shift depending on who is in the room, even when the substance stays the same. Getting the substance right and the register wrong still counts as getting it wrong.
  • Structured verbal delivery. A separate skill from writing well. Writing gives you time to revise. Speaking gives you one pass, in front of people, with no edit window.

So I joined Toastmasters. My first speech was the Icebreaker, and I titled it It All Starts with a Question.

Underneath all three is a habit I picked up from research. I am passionate about social network analysis, mapping relationships structurally, identifying where connections are strong, where they are absent, and what those patterns mean for outcomes. The same lens works on myself. Where am I already operating with credibility and effectiveness? Where are the gaps that would expand my range if closed? The goal is not a flattering map. It is an accurate one.

Growth as a professional practice is iterative and undramatic. It looks like a conversation that went better than it would have a year ago. It looks like catching yourself defaulting to an old pattern, then adjusting mid-interaction. It looks like feedback that still stings a little, which usually means it was accurate. You mostly notice it in retrospect.

I am not done. I do not expect to be. That is not a limitation, that is the design.
